inventionTitles.title: Artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for wireless communications
用于无线通信的人工智能和机器学习技术

section.content: 提供了用于无线通信的人工智能和机器学习技术。本申请涉及设备和部件，包括用于应用功能(AF)直接接入无线电接入网络(RAN)管理功能的装置、系统和方法。

Artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for wireless communications are provided. The present application relates to devices and components, including apparatuses, systems and methods for Application Function (AF) direct access Radio Access Network (RAN) management functions.

Artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques for wireless communicationsCross-reference to other applications

The present application claims priority from U.S. provisional application No. 63/541,620, entitled "ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND MACHINE LEARNING TECHNOLOGIES FOR WIRELESS COMMUNICATION," filed on 9/29, 2023, which is incorporated herein by reference in its entirety for all purposes.

Technical Field

The present application relates generally to communication networks and, in particular, to techniques for affecting network functions by applying functions.

Background

Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AIML) can be used in wireless communications to automate tasks, optimize network resources, or predict and alleviate problems. The AIML model may be used to optimize Radio Resource Management (RRM) parameters such as channel allocation, power control or scheduling. AIML may be used for mobility management, interference management, or security threat detection.

For example, the AIML model and algorithms may be used in 3GPP networks in the context of network slicing. AIML can be used to automate the deployment and management of network slices.

Detailed Description

The following detailed description refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numbers may be used in different drawings to identify the same or similar elements. In the following description, for purposes of explanation and not limitation, specific details are set forth such as particular structures, architectures, interfaces, and/or techniques in order to provide a thorough understanding of the various aspects of some embodiments. However, it will be apparent to one skilled in the art having the benefit of this disclosure that the various aspects may be practiced in other examples that depart from these specific details. In some instances, descriptions of well-known devices, circuits, and methods are omitted so as not to obscure the description of the various aspects with unnecessary detail. For the purposes of this document, the phrase "a or B" refers to (a), (B) or (a and B), and the phrase "based on a" refers to "based at least in part on a", e.g., it may be "based only on a" or it may be "based in part on a".

The following is a glossary of terms that may be used in this disclosure.

As used herein, the term "circuitry" refers to, is part of, or includes hardware components such as electronic circuitry, logic circuitry, a processor (shared, dedicated, or group) or memory (shared, dedicated, or group) configured to provide the described functionality, an Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), a Field Programmable Device (FPD) (e.g., a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), a Programmable Logic Device (PLD), a Complex PLD (CPLD), a high-capacity PLD (hcpll), a structured ASIC, or a system-on-a-chip (SoC)), and/or a Digital Signal Processor (DSP). In some aspects, circuitry may execute one or more software or firmware programs to provide at least some of the described functionality. The term "circuitry" may also refer to a combination of one or more hardware elements and program code for performing the functionality of the program code (or a combination of circuitry used in an electrical or electronic system). In these aspects, a combination of hardware elements and program code may be referred to as a particular type of circuit.

As used herein, the term "processor circuit" refers to, is part of, or includes circuitry capable of sequentially and automatically performing a series of arithmetic or logical operations, or recording, storing, or communicating digital data. The term "processor circuit" may refer to an application processor, a baseband processor, a Central Processing Unit (CPU), a graphics processing unit, a single-core processor, a dual-core processor, a three-core processor, a four-core processor, or any other device capable of executing or otherwise operating computer-executable instructions (such as program code), a software module, or a functional process.

As used herein, the term "interface circuit" refers to, is part of, or includes a circuit that enables the exchange of information between two or more components or devices. The term "interface circuit" may refer to one or more hardware interfaces, such as a bus, an I/O interface, a peripheral interface, a network interface card, and the like.

As used herein, the term "user equipment" or "UE" refers to a device of a remote user that has radio communication capabilities and may describe network resources in a communication network. The terms "user equipment" or "UE" may be considered synonymous and may be referred to as a client, mobile phone, mobile device, mobile terminal, user terminal, mobile unit, mobile station, mobile user, subscriber, user, remote station, access agent, user agent, receiver, radio equipment, reconfigurable mobile device, etc. Furthermore, the term "user equipment" or "UE" may include any type of wireless/wired device or any computing device that includes a wireless communication interface.

As used herein, the term "computer system" refers to any type of interconnected electronic device, computer device, or component thereof. In addition, the term "computer system" or "system" may refer to various components of a computer that are communicatively coupled to each other. Furthermore, the term "computer system" or "system" may refer to a plurality of computer devices or a plurality of computing systems communicatively coupled to each other and configured to share computing resources or networking resources.

As used herein, the term "resource" refers to a physical or virtual device, a physical or virtual component within a computing environment, or a physical or virtual component within a particular device, such as a computer device, a mechanical device, a memory space, a processor/CPU time, a processor/CPU utilization, a processor and accelerator load, a hardware time or usage, electrical power, input/output operations, ports or network sockets, channel/link allocations, throughput, memory usage, storage, a network, databases and application programs, workload units, and the like. "hardware resources" may refer to computer, storage, or network resources provided by physical hardware elements. "virtualized resources" may refer to computer, storage, or network resources provided by a virtualization infrastructure to an application, device, system, or the like. The term "network resource" or "communication resource" may refer to a resource that is accessible to a computer device/system via a communication network. The term "system resource" may refer to any kind of shared entity that provides a service and may include computing resources or network resources. A system resource may be considered a set of contiguous functions, network data objects, or services that are accessible through a server, where such system resource resides on a single host or multiple hosts and is clearly identifiable.

As used herein, the term "channel" refers to any tangible or intangible transmission medium for transmitting data or a data stream. The term "channel" may be synonymous or equivalent to "communication channel," "data communication channel," "transmission channel," "data transmission channel," "access channel," "data access channel," "link," "data link," "carrier," "radio frequency carrier," or any other similar term representing a pathway or medium through which data is transmitted. In addition, as used herein, the term "link" refers to a connection made between two devices for transmitting and receiving information.

As used herein, the term "cause. Instantiation": "instantiation" and the like refer to the creation of an instance. "instance" also refers to a specific occurrence of an object, which may occur, for example, during execution of program code.

The term "connected" may mean that two or more elements at a common communication protocol layer have an established signaling relationship with each other through a communication channel, link, interface, or reference point.

As used herein, the term "network element" refers to physical or virtualized equipment or infrastructure for providing wired or wireless communication network services. The term "network element" may be considered synonymous to or referred to as a networked computer, networking hardware, network equipment, network node, virtualized network function, etc.

The term "information element" refers to a structural element that contains one or more fields. The term "field" refers to a single content of an information element or a data element containing content. The information elements may include one or more additional information elements.

Fig. 1 illustrates a network environment 100 according to some embodiments. The network environment 100 may include a UE 104 coupled with a Base Station (BS) 108 of a Radio Access Network (RAN). In some embodiments, BS108 is a next generation node B (gNB) that provides one or more 3GPP New Radio (NR) cells. In other embodiments, BS108 is an evolved node B (eNB) that provides one or more Long Term Evolution (LTE) cells. The air interface over which the UE 104 and BS108 communicate may be compatible with 3GPP Technical Specifications (TS), such as those defining fifth generation (5G) NR or later system standards (e.g., sixth generation (6G) standards).

Network environment 100 may include a network 105. The network 105 may provide services, such as voice or data connectivity, to the UE 104. The network 105 may include a Core Network (CN) 106 or a BS108. The CN 106 may connect the BS108 and the UE 104 to other entities, such as an Edge Data Network (EDN), the internet, or an Application Function (AF) 102. The CN 106 may be responsible for call and session configuration or control, mobility management, or service provisioning.

The CN 106 may include one or more network functions, such as a network open function (network exposure function, NEF) 116 or a network function NF 112.NF 112 is a general network function and may represent any network function provided by CN 106. NF 112 may manage or control the operation of the network nodes. For example, NF 112 may be a RAN management function that controls the operation and configuration of BS108 or UE 104.

AF 102 may be a functional element that may provide information related to a service or application to other network functions. In some examples, AF 102 is a function managed by a network operator. In some examples, AF 102 may be a third party function residing in a cloud or third party server.

AF 102 may be coupled to network 105 through CN 106. AF 102 may be coupled with NEF 116. In some embodiments, the AF 102 may be coupled with NF 112. In some examples, AF 102 may communicate with NF 112 through NEF 116, e.g., AF 102 may send a message to NEF 116, and NEF 116 may forward the message to NF 112. In some examples, the AF 102 may communicate directly with the NF 112, e.g., the AF 102 may send a message directly to the NF 112.

The UE 104 may be communicatively coupled with the BS108 by a communication link 170. The UE 104 may collect data related to the communication link 170 or other information related to the UE 104. The collected data may be associated with the end user's intent, context, or intended action. For example, in an in-car V2X system, a UE (e.g., a vehicle) may have information related to a user's lane crossing intent, level of distraction, or destination. The UE 104 may also receive information from the network 105, other UEs, or other data networks. The UE 104 may use this data to predict a configuration, such as a traffic profile or an operating mode. The UE 104 may use AIML models to analyze the information and obtain predictions or results.

The UE 104 may process the data and generate AIML data 110. The UE may share AIML data 110 with the AF 102. The UE 104 may share the processed results 120 with the AF 102. The processed results 120 may include a predictive, inferred, or AIML model developed by the UE 104 or an application or function associated with the UE 104.

AF 102 may interact with network 105 to obtain authorization to access entities and elements associated with network 105. AF 102 may affect the operation of network 105 through its interaction with NEF 116 or NF 112. For example, AF 102 may affect traffic routing of an application and interact with a Policy Control Function (PCF) to enable policy control. NEF 116 may provide means for AF 102 to access network capabilities and resources. By opening capabilities (e.g., network functions or resources), the NEF 116 or AF 102 may affect how the opened NFs or resources operate or interact with each other. AF 102 may affect data session configuration, traffic routing, or quality of service (QoS) parameters. The network 105 may send the configuration 160 to the UE 104 based on the AF 102 impact.

In some embodiments, the AF 102 may affect mobility, session management policies, and configurations associated with the BS 108 or UE 104.

In some embodiments, the AF 102 may act on behalf of the UE 104 to affect operation of the network 105 based on information or inferences of the UE.

The network 105 may authorize the AF 102 to access the NEF 116 or NF 112. The network 105 may send an information openness 150 to the AF 102. The information openings 150 may include data applicable or associated with AIML models or analyses. The information openings 150 may include a list of NFs or resources that the AF 102 is authorized to access or affect.

AF 102 may provide AF impact data 140 to network 105. The AF impact data 140 can include raw data (e.g., measurement data), analytical data (e.g., AIML data or processed results), or AIML models or parameters.

Due to privacy concerns, it may be desirable for the UE 104 or AF 102 to maintain raw measurements or data in the device. Locally running AIML may generate results and inferences based on the data. Affecting the direct access of the NF 112 may enable the UE 104 or AF 102 to perform real-time or near real-time procedures or support applications that may require a fast control loop.

Fig. 2 illustrates an operational flow/algorithm 200 structure according to some embodiments. Operational flow/algorithm structure 200 is an example of the AF 102 affecting the operation of network 105. The operational flow/algorithm structure 200 may be implemented by a network node (e.g., network node 1000) or a component therein (e.g., processor 1004).

Operational flow/algorithm structure 200 may include performing AF authorization at 210. The AF may be an example of AF 102 in FIG. 1. The AF authorization may be performed by a Mobile Network Operator (MNO) or by a UE (e.g., UE 104 in fig. 1).

The AF may be a component of a third party service that interacts with a core network (e.g., CN 106 in fig. 1) to affect network operation. The authorization procedure of the AF may ensure that the AF has the necessary permissions to interact with the network.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 200 may include determining aspects that may be affected by AF at 220. For example, the AF may request access to the NF. The network may perform authorization including the user agreeing to the management operation to determine whether the AF access is granted and to determine the access range.

User consent management may involve obtaining explicit permission from the user before the AF may access or use certain information or services on behalf of the UE. Consent management may be necessary in handling sensitive information or operations that may affect user experience or privacy. For example, the AF may request access to the user's network slice. The network may need to ensure that the AF is authorized to access only certain network slices and prevent it from accessing information of other network slices. The authorization process may involve obtaining consent from the user.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 200 may include discovering available services or functions at 230. For example, the AF may discover available services through the NEF. The available services may be associated with services that the AF has access to or affects.

Service discovery may involve an AF querying a network to determine available services. This may include communication with various NFs such as Network Repository Functions (NRFs) or NEFs.

The operational flow/algorithm structure 200 may include discovering and connecting to an NF associated with the RAN (e.g., a RAN management function or RAN NF) at 240 for real-time, non-real-time or near real-time impact.

The AF may send impact data, such as raw data, AIML models, or UE-initiated data or models, to the NF. The NF may consider AF inputs (e.g., impact data) or data from other NFs (e.g., network data analysis function (NWDAF)).

The AF may affect network operation through a parameter provisioning procedure. The AF may provide parameters to the network by, for example, provisioning parameters to the NEF or other NF. The receiving NF may use the received parameters to determine configuration parameters or network operation. For example, the AF may provide some physical layer (PHY) configuration to the RAN NF. The RAN NF may use PHY configuration to configure the UE, e.g., via Radio Resource Control (RRC) configuration signaling.

AIML provisioning may include obtaining UE (or end user) consent. The consent may be a full consent provided to a particular AF, or it may be a granular consent provided in terms of the action or aspect being affected. The agreement may apply to a particular time period or geographic location. The UE agrees to be updatable through network or application layer signaling (e.g., over The Top (OTT) signaling).

The AIML-based provisioning may provide granularity control of UE configuration. For example, accessing the RAN through AF or AF on behalf of the UE, the UE may affect RAN parameters. The direct access RAN may implement a fast control loop for near real time operation. The AF may access the RAN node directly or through a local NEF (e.g., local to the RAN node). For example, the AF may access AIML RAN NF, such as a RAN AI/ML model or data repository function or a RAN AIML model or data coordination function. The parameter provisioning may mask aspects related to user intent, sensitive or private information (e.g., identifiers), or system information (e.g., application or device settings that are considered private).

The receiving NF may associate or combine the parameter supply input from the AF with NWDAF. For example, the MNO may combine the AF input with the analysis from NWDAF. The network may provide the relevant NWDAF analysis to the AF. The AF may combine or associate NWDAF analyses and incorporate them into the parameter supply, or the AF may provide NWDAF analysis to the UE and the UE may consider NWDAF analysis in triggering the parameter supply.

The AF may use parameter provisioning to affect CN parameters. For example, the AF may affect UE operation mode, long-term UE behavior (e.g., UE subscription for slicing), or short-term behavior (e.g., session lifetime or QoS flow lifetime). The AF may affect CN mobility management policies such as suggested registration areas, periodicity of Mobility Registration Update (MRU) messages, or parameters associated with radio link failure. AF may affect CN to dynamically change semantic traffic flow characteristics.

The AF may use parameter provisioning to affect RAN configuration. For example, the AF may affect duty cycle, preferred carrier aggregation configuration, measurement configuration for power saving, radio resource allocation, beamforming selection, RRM, RAN mobility configuration including beam groups, or Transmission and Reception Point (TRP) selection. AF may affect AIML modes at NF.

AF may affect networks in device-to-device (D2D) communications. For example, the AF may affect parameters associated with D2D grant, side link UE selection, routing, or side link RRM.

AF may affect open RAN (ora) functionality across rApp, xApp, SMO, A, E2, or O1. For example, AF may affect ORAN Xn-based multi-gNB coordination. rApp, xApp, SMO, A1, E2, O1 or Xn interfaces are ORAN services or interfaces according to the ORAN specification.

The AF may influence the network policy through parameter provisioning. For example, the AF may recommend AIML that the policy select or affect NF associated with a UE Known Performance Indicator (KPI), failure, or error rate.

Fig. 3 illustrates a signaling diagram 300 according to some embodiments. The signaling diagram 300 may be an example of a provisioning procedure for setting up a UE operating profile. The UE operating profile may include a set of UE configurations, such as radio access capabilities, network capabilities, or mobility preferences. For example, the UE or AF may affect network decisions related to mobility update timers, allowed network slices, or radio configurations. The UE may register one or more operating profiles with the network. Based on AIML inferences, AIML functions at the UE or AF may determine and select an operational profile. For example, AIML inferences can be based upon knowledge or information regarding AIML capabilities or available datasets. The UE or AF may call the NEF API to supply a configuration corresponding to the UE operating profile.

At 320, the UE 104 may send a registration request to the AF 102. For example, AIML clients in the UE may register with the AF to trigger authorization or login to MNO NEF 116. The UE may send a UE registration request using application layer signaling. The registration request or another message may include a list of provisioning parameters and an consent input (e.g., one or more indications of one or more consents).

At 325, the AF 102 may check whether authorization exists. If no authorization is associated with NEF 116, AF 102 may send an authorization request message to NEF 116. For example, AF 102 may use Nnef _ AFAuthorization _request message to Request authorization from NEF 116. The authorization request message may include a UE Identifier (ID), a list of allowed UE provisioning parameters that AF 102 has received user consent.

At 330, NEF 116 may perform authorization in response to the authorization request message from AF 102. The NEF 116 may use the consent input and information associated with consent retrieved from the Unified Data Management (UDM) 314 to authorize the AF 102. The UDM may be a network node or NF that manages data for network users. For example, the NEF 116 may retrieve UE consent information stored in the UDM.

At 335, NEF 116 may send an authorization acknowledgement message to AF 102. For example, NEF 116 may use Nnef _ AFAuthorization _confirm message to inform AF 102 whether AF 102 is authorized to access NEF 116 or other NFs. The authorization confirmation message may include an indication, e.g., authorization information, indicating that AF 102 is authorized to access NEF 116 or other NF. The authorization confirmation message may include the authorization ID. When accessing the NEF 116 or other NF, the AF 102 may use the authorization ID to indicate that it has authorization. The authorization acknowledgement may include a validity time that may indicate a duration of time that the authorization is valid. The AF 102 may configure a timer based on the validity time.

At 340, based on AIML inference, AIML client in UE 104 may trigger AF 102 for parameter provisioning. The UE 104 may send a trigger to the AF 102 using application layer signaling. The trigger may include an indication of an operating mode of the UE. The trigger may be based on an inference or partial inference result. Inference or triggers may be combined with other inference results at AF. Other inferences at the aF may be provided by the core network NF (e.g., NWDAF, RAN-related NF, or other CN NF).

At 345, the AF 102 invokes a parameter provisioning service at NF. AF 102 may invoke the parameter provisioning service at NEF 116 by sending a provisioning request message to NEF 116. For example, AF 102 may send Nnef _ ParameterProvision _request message to NEF 116. The provisioning request message may include an indication associated with the AF 102 authorization ID, the UE ID, and provisioning parameters, such as an indication of a preferred operating profile of the UE. The time may be associated with a validity duration or a scheduling time. For example, the time indication may determine when the requested operational profile may be applied.

At 350, NEF 116 may determine whether AF 102 has authorization to invoke the requested service. The NEF 116 may retrieve AF 102 authorization information from the UDM 314. For example, NEF 116 can retrieve the supplied operating profile from UDM 314.

At 355, NEF 116 may send a parameter provisioning confirm message to AF 102. For example, NEF 116 can send Nnef-ParameterProvision _Confirm message to AF 102.

At 360, NEF 116 may invoke an access and mobility management function (AMF) service for parameter provisioning. The NEF 116 may invoke the AMF service for provisioning by sending a provisioning request message to the AMF 312. The AMF 312 may be a function of the CN. For example, NEF 116 can send Namf _ UEParameterProvision _request message to AMF 312. The NEF 116 may send a provisioning request message to the AMF registered by the UE 104. The provisioning request message may include the UE ID, an indication of the preferred operating profile of the UE, and a validity time.

At 365, the AMF 312 may invoke RAN Management Function (RMF) 318 services to update the UE context to provision the updated UE context parameters. RAN management functions may be associated with UE 104 and BS108 in fig. 1. The AF 312 may send an update request message to the RMF 318 to update the UE context with the provided UE context parameters. The UE context parameters may include an indication of a preferred operating profile of the UE. For example, the AMF 312 may send Nran _ UEContext _ UpdateReq to the BS 108.

At 370, RMF 318 may update the UE 104 configuration according to the updated UE context parameters. For example, the RMF 318 may update the UE 104 by instructing a BS (e.g., BS108 in fig. 1) to send a Radio Resource Control (RRC) reconfiguration message to update the RRC configuration of the UE according to the operating profile indicated by the updated UE context.

Fig. 4 illustrates a network environment 400 according to some embodiments. The network is an example of the NF of the CN 106 available on the service bus 480. The service bus 480 may be used to facilitate communication between the connected NFs and the AFs 102.

In some examples, session Management Function (SMF) 410 may be connected to service bus 480. The SMF 410 may be responsible for session establishment, modification, or release.

In some examples, registration function 420 may be connected to service bus 480. Registration function 420 may be responsible for managing registration of a UE or AF (e.g., AF 102).

In some examples, authentication function (AUSF) 430 may be connected to service bus 480.AUSF 430,430 may support authentication for access to a network (e.g., network 105 in fig. 1) by trusted or untrusted entities.

In some examples, policy management function (PCF) 440 may be connected to service bus 480.PCF 440 may control parameters that regulate user data traffic.

In some examples, RMF 318 may be connected to service bus 480. The RAN management functions may control and configure the operation of the RAN (including BS108 and UE 104 in fig. 1).

In some examples, the analysis function 460 (e.g., NWDAF) may be connected to the service bus 480. The analysis function 460 may provide analysis to the core network NF and operation and maintenance (O & M).

In some examples, a User Plane Function (UPF) 470 may be connected to a service bus 480. The UPF 470 may be responsible for handling user plane data traffic.

AF 102 may directly invoke NF connected to service bus 480. For example, the AF 102 may directly invoke RAN services for updated UE-selected configurations by sending parameter provisioning requests directly to the RMF 318. The NF on the direct access service bus 480 reduces the latency and overhead of AF 102 requests compared to requests handled by the NEF.

The NEF may provide the authorization and user consent checks required before allowing the AF 102 to invoke NF services directly on the service bus 480. Once authorized, the AF 102 may be allowed to interact directly with the NF (e.g., the RMF 318). The authentication timer may regulate direct access. For example, the AF 102 may be allowed to interact directly with the NF on the service bus 480 within a predetermined timer. Other events such as UE mobility, cell reselection, or other network conditions may affect the direct access of the AF 102 to the NF.

Fig. 5 illustrates a signaling diagram 500 according to some embodiments. The signaling diagram 500 is an example of a provisioning procedure for setting up a UE-selected RAN configuration through a direct interface to the RMF 318.

The UE 104 may select a RAN configuration. The RAN configuration may include PHY or RRC configuration. The UE 104 may select the RAN configuration based on AIML operations (e.g., based on AIML requirements and capabilities and the UE's knowledge of current and future requirements).

The UE 104 may provide AIML the processing results or the selected preferred RAN configuration to AIML AF. The UE may provide the RMF 318 with authorized metadata or enriched information to enable the RMF 318 to perform RAN configuration selection.

AF 102 may invoke the NEF API to discover RAN nodes to which the UE is connected or registered. The NEF may also authorize the AF 102 and check for consent of the user to the effect of the UE behaviour.

The authorized AF 102 may initiate the establishment of AIML sessions with the RMF 318. The AF 102 may send metadata or an indication of the selected RAN configuration directly to the RMF 318.

At 520, the UE 104 may send a registration request to the AF 102. For example, AIML clients in the UE may register with the AF to trigger authorization or login to MNO NEF 116. The UE may send a UE registration request using application layer signaling. The registration request or another message may include a list of provisioning parameters and a consent input.

At 525, the AF 102 may check whether authorization exists. If no authorization is associated with NEF 116, AF 102 may send an authorization request message to NEF 116. For example, AF 102 may use Nnef _ AFAuthorization _request message to Request authorization from NEF 116. The authorization request message may include a UE Identifier (ID), an indication of the type of updated AIML session with RMF 318, a list of allowed UE provisioning parameters that AF 102 has received user consent, user consent input, and a request for a RAN controller identifier. The RAN controller identifier may be an address for directly invoking the service-based interface from the RAN node. Generally, when the direct connection points to NF, the controller identifier may be an address of NF associated with the UE, such as an IP address or URI.

At 530, NEF 116 may perform authorization in response to the authorization request message from AF 102. The NEF 116 may use the consent input and information associated with consent retrieved from the Unified Data Management (UDM) 314 to authorize the AF 102. The UDM may be a network node or NF that manages data for network users. For example, the NEF 116 may retrieve UE consent information stored in the UDM.

At 535, the NEF 116 may send a request to the AMF 312 to which the UE 104 is currently registered to retrieve the relevant RMF identifier that should receive the RAN configuration. The RMF identifier may be an Internet Protocol (IP) address or a Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) associated with the RMF or RAN node. Generally, when the direct connection points to NF, the controller identifier may be an address of NF associated with the UE, such as an IP address or URI.

At 540, NEF 116 may send an authorization acknowledgement message to AF 102. For example, the NEF 116 may use Nnef _ AFAuthorization _confirm message to inform the AF 102 whether the AF 102 is authorized to access the NEF 116 or other NFs (e.g., RMF 318). The authorization acknowledgement message may include an indication that the AF 102 is authorized to access the NEF 116 or other NF. The authorization confirmation message may include the authorization ID. When accessing the NEF 116 or other NF (e.g., RMF 318), the AF 102 may use the authorization ID to indicate that it has authorization. The authorization acknowledgement may include a validity time that may indicate a duration of time that the authorization is valid. The AF 102 may configure a timer based on the validity time. The authorization acknowledgement may include an RMF address. The RMF address may indicate that the RAN configured RMF should be received. The RMF address may be an IP address or URI of the RMF or corresponding RAN node.

At 545, based on AIML inference, AIML client in UE 104 may trigger AF 102 to initiate or modify AIML session. The UE 104 may send a trigger to the AF 102 using application layer signaling. The trigger may include an AF 102 authorization ID, a UE ID, or an indication of the selected RAN configuration of the UE.

At 550, the AF 102 may invoke RAN services for UE configuration provisioning at RMF 318. The AF 102 may invoke the parameter provisioning service at RMF 318 by sending AIML a session request to RMF 318. For example, the AF 102 may send Nran _ AIMLSession _create/NModify _request messages to the RMF 318. The session request message may include an indication associated with the AF 102 authorization ID, the UE ID, and an indication of the UE configuration provisioning (e.g., an indication of the selected RAN configuration of the UE).

At 555, RMF 318 may receive the UE-selected RAN configuration and validate the request. For example, RMF 318 may use the AF authorization ID received in the session request message to verify the RAN configuration selected by the UE. RMF 318 may retrieve information about the registered RAN configuration of the UE from UDM 314.

At 560, based on the successful verification at 555, RMF 318 may send an acknowledgement message to AF 102. For example, RMF 318 may send Nran _ AIMLSession _create_confirm message to AF 102. The acknowledgement message may include the session ID.

At 565, RMF 318 may update the UE 104 configuration according to the received selected RAN configuration. For example, the RMF 318 may update the UE 104 by instructing a BS (e.g., BS108 in fig. 1) to send a Radio Resource Control (RRC) reconfiguration message to update the UE's RRC configuration according to the selected RAN configuration indicated by the session request message.

Fig. 6 illustrates an operational flow/algorithm structure 600 according to some embodiments. Operational flow/algorithm structure 600 is an example of a NEF that grants an AF access to an NF. The operational flow/algorithm structure 600 may be implemented by a network node (e.g., CN 106 or network node 1000) or a component therein (e.g., processor 1004).

Operational flow/algorithm structure 600 may include receiving an authorization request from an AF at 610. The authorization request may be associated with access to the NF. The access to the NF may be either an indirect access through the NEF or a direct access.

The request may be a request to access NF on the service bus. For example, the request may be a request to access RMF.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 600 may include determining whether the AF is authorized to access the NF at 620. The NEF may request and receive a message from the UDM including an indication of consent associated with the UE. The NEF may request and receive a message from the AMF including an indication of an identifier of a network function associated with the UE. The NEF may determine whether the AF is authorized to access the NF based on an indication of consent received from the UDM or an indication of a network identifier received from the AMF.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 600 may include transmitting an acknowledgement message to the AF indicating that the AF is authorized to access the NF at 630. The acknowledgement message may include a validity timer that may indicate how long the AF authorization is valid.

The NEF may also perform a parameter provisioning procedure. The NEF may receive a provisioning request from the AF. The NEF may determine that the AF is authorized to invoke the parameter provisioning service at the NEF. If the AF is successfully authorized, the NEF may send an acknowledgment message to the AF.

The NEF and AF may establish AIML sessions. The AIML session may provide the AF with an opening to partial inferences from the NF. In some examples NWDA NF may provide partial results to the AF. The AIML session may provide provisioning of configuration parameters to the AF. In direct access, the AF may establish AIML a session with the NF.

Fig. 7 illustrates an operational flow/algorithm structure 700 according to some embodiments. Operational flow/algorithm structure 700 is an example of an RMF that establishes direct access to an AF. The operational flow/algorithm structure 700 may be implemented by a network node (e.g., CN 106, BS108, or network node 1000) or a component therein (e.g., processor 1004).

Operational flow/algorithm structure 700 may include receiving a session request from an AF at 710, wherein the request is associated with a UE. The session request may include the UE ID and an authorization ID associated with the AF. The session request may include a configuration associated with the UE.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 700 may include sending an acknowledgement response to the AF at 720. The acknowledgement response may include the session ID.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 700 may include configuring a UE based on a session request at 730. For example, the RMF may instruct the BS to transmit an RRC reconfiguration message to the UE based on the UE configuration in the session request message.

Fig. 8 illustrates an operational flow/algorithm structure 800 in accordance with some embodiments. Operational flow/algorithm structure 800 is an example of a UE establishing direct access to RMF. The operational flow/algorithm structure 800 may be implemented by a UE (e.g., UE 104 or UE 900) or a component therein (e.g., processing circuitry 904).

Operational flow/algorithm structure 800 may include sending a registration request to an AF at 810. The registration request may include one or more indications associated with the UE's consent.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 800 may include sending a trigger to initiate AIML a session at 820. The trigger may include an indication of the configuration selected by the UE. The configuration of UE selection may include mobility management policy, duty cycle, carrier aggregation configuration, measurement configuration, radio Resource Management (RRM) configuration, RAN mobility configuration, AIML model selection indication, resource allocation indication, or beamforming selection indication.

Operational flow/algorithm structure 800 may include receiving a reconfiguration message from the RAN at 830. The reconfiguration message may be based on a configuration selected by the UE. In one example, the reconfiguration message may be an RRC reconfiguration message.
